title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs
claim: Time-dependent systems exhibit several distinct kinds of non-stationarity, such as abrupt shocks, slow structural drift and limited observation windows, that break standard assumptions.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, each a time-series sketch with a time axis
description: Three side-by-side schematic time-series sketches, labeled (a), (b) and (c). Each has black axes with arrowheads and a time axis t. Panel (a) shows a jagged black line over the years 2004 to 2010 that drops sharply at a vertical red dotted line near 2008, which marks a sudden shock such as a market crash. Panel (b) shows two sinusoidal segments separated by an axis break, one around 1851 to 1852 at a low level and one around 2024 to 2025 at a higher level, which marks a long-term structural shift as in climate data. Panel (c) shows a smooth decaying curve with a light pink rectangle labeled 'Development' and 'Testing', which marks a limited observation window that ends before the curve's later behavior. The red dotted line and the pink box are the only color and draw the eye first.
caption: Examples of different types of non-stationarity that can arise in time-dependent systems. (a) Sudden distribution shift due to external shocks, illustrated by a stock market crash. (b) Long-term structural changes, as in climate time series. (c) Limited observation window during system development, where calibration and testing occur on different parts of the trajectory.
abstract: Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.
